It has accompanied festivals such as Nowruz, court playing and prayer chanting, and it entered Sufi ritual; in conservative Sunni communities women used it for celebrations and men for warfare. In India the daf and the smaller dafli are folk instruments, and the daf later appeared in protest and in Bollywood. The source also mentions the khosravani composed by Babad, and the riq's place beside the ney and the chang in large orchestral ensembles.
裡格手鼓與達夫同屬框鼓，其波斯語名「達普」見於中古波斯語，維吾爾傳統音樂也有相近: The riq and the daf are both frame drums; the Persian name dap is found in Middle Persian, and traditional Uyghur music uses a similar name. Paintings from before the common era and the Behistun inscription of the sixth to fifth century BC show that it existed before Islam and Sufism arose. In the Sasanian period it was used at festivals such as Nowruz, in Iranian classical music and for court modes, which were later handed down as the radif and dastgah systems. It reached medieval Europe through the ancient Middle East, Greece, Rome and Islamic culture; the Arabs brought it to Spain, and the Ottomans introduced it to Europe again in the seventeenth century. Conservative Sunnis regard it as an instrument allowed to women for celebrations and to men for the battlefield, and Sufi ritual values it too.

Its range lies in the middle and upper frequencies: striking the centre of the head gives a crisp, strong main tone, while the edge gives a softer sound. The metal jingles set in the frame ring like small bells as they vibrate and blend with the low resonance of the head, producing a richly layered sound. Compared with the heaviness of a Western drum kit, the riq is lighter and more nimble; set against the warm, muffled tone of an earthen drum, its sound has a brighter folk character. The instrument is strong in both rhythm and melody: it can carry complex rhythmic movement, and different striking positions give it many tone colours.

The riq and the daf are alternative names or variants of the same frame drum, a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.311. It has a round wooden frame, metal frames also appearing in modern instruments, with rectangular slots holding small metal cymbals or jingles, and one side is covered with fish skin, goatskin or a synthetic head. It is played with the drum held in the left hand, which strikes the rim, while the right hand strikes the centre; a finger of the right hand is hooked behind the next and suddenly released, like a finger snap, which produces a fast, sharp sound. It is common in the traditional, classical and popular music of the Middle East, of regions under Persian influence, and of South and Central Asia, and it is also used at festivals, in Sufi ritual, on the battlefield and on folk occasions.
裡格手鼓／達夫的琴身傳統為圓形木框，現代亦見金屬框；框上以三或四個長方形孔固定薄: The body of the riq and the daf is traditionally a round wooden frame, with metal frames also seen today; three or four rectangular slots in the frame hold thin metal plates or rings as jingles. The head is thin, semi-transparent fish skin or goatskin, and synthetic materials have been used in recent times. The wooden frame can be softened in water and then bent around a hot metal cylinder, with the ends glued together; the head is held by another wooden frame or by nails. A variant arranges ring-shaped jingles around the inner rim.
